summary: Defines a way for a user interface to reach a textual, DAP-like directory interface over a TCP connection. It is described as a local mechanism and is informational, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary:
X.500's directory service can look up people, resources and organisations. Reaching it normally means speaking a heavy protocol from the OSI stack, and small machines could not afford the code for that.

This memo describes a workaround: run the heavy protocol on one machine and expose a plain text front end on another, so that a simple program can drive the directory.

subtitle: A simple text protocol for accessing X.500 directory services.

tldr.problem: The X.500 directory is powerful but its access protocol, DAP, needs the full OSI stack, which is too much code to fit on a small workstation or a personal computer.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes a split model. A Directory Assistant on a capable machine holds the DAP implementation and exports a plain text protocol over TCP, and a small client on the other machine speaks that.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that records a protocol already in use, and it says explicitly that it specifies no standard.

facts.label: Letter response codes
facts.value: m, y, p, e, l, d and P

today: RFC 1202 is an Informational document from February 1991 and has not been obsoleted. The memo documents a protocol that already existed, calls the mechanism a local one, and says it does not specify any standard.

sections.title: The Problem and the Split Model
sections.content:
The OSI Directory provides a powerful infrastructure for the retrieval of information objects. This infrastructure can be used to support white pages applications, application entity lookup and so on. The Directory service is provided to applications through the Directory Access Protocol, which binds a Directory User Agent to a Directory System Agent.

The DAP is an OSI application layer protocol which uses the rich OSI upper-layer infrastructure. Unfortunately, the coding investment to implement the DAP is significant, so it is difficult to host applications using the Directory on smaller workstations and personal computers.

The memo details a local mechanism which has been successfully used to separate the functionality of the DAP from the complexity of implementing it. A split-DUA model is used: the DAP is implemented on an entity, the Directory Assistant, which resides on a capable workstation or mainframe and exports a simpler interface, the Directory Assistance protocol, to other end-systems where the user interface resides, termed the DA-client. Since this mechanism provides assistance to applications wishing to access the Directory, it is termed the Directory Assistance service.

The memo also notes that it documents an already existing protocol, which was originally used to provide a split-DUA model within the same host. In the absence of detailed historical and implementational understanding, some of the mechanisms described may not appear intuitive.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is a helper on the big machine. The small machine asks the helper a simple question, and the helper does the hard directory work on its behalf.

sections.title: The Two Connections
sections.content:
The DA service operates using two TCP connections, a control connection and a data connection. The control connection defines the lifetime of an instance of the DA service. Throughout this lifetime, several data connections may be established, but at any given instant between zero and one data connections will be in progress.

The service is provided by the Directory Assistant, which consists of two entities: a DA-server, which manages the control connection, and a DAP-listener, which responds to commands on the data connection. The DA-server oversees the behavior of the DAP-listener.

Data sent over the control connection consists of a series of transactions expressed in NVT-ASCII. Each transaction consists of the client sending a directive, a line of text terminated by CR-LF, and the DA-server returning a response, also a line of text terminated by CR-LF. All responses from a DA-server start with either +OK or -ERR, depending on whether the transaction was successful. A DA-server listens on TCP port 411 for incoming connections. Upon establishing a control connection it returns a response indicating whether the service has been started. If successful, the response contains an IP address and a TCP port, expressed in NVT-ASCII and separated by one or more spaces, corresponding to the TCP endpoint that the DAP-listener will use for the data connection. The DA-server and DAP-listener need not reside at the same IP address. If the service cannot be started, an error response is returned and the control connection is closed.

There are three commands on the control connection. The INTR command takes no arguments and is used to interrupt any DAP transaction currently in progress; it always returns success. The STAT command takes no arguments and is used to verify that the DAP-listener is available, returning success only if the DAP-listener is still active. The QUIT command takes no arguments and is used to terminate the DA service; it always returns success.
sections.plainLanguage: One connection stays open for the life of the session and carries housekeeping. The other is opened and closed for each query, and the server tells the client which port to use for it.

sections.title: The Data Connection and Its Responses
sections.content:
Data sent over a data connection consists of a single DAP transaction, expressed in NVT-ASCII. Each transaction consists of the client sending a command, a line of text terminated by the LF character, and the DAP-listener returning zero or more responses, each with a specific termination sequence. All responses from a DAP-listener start with a single identifying character. If the character is a digit, the termination sequence consists of closing the data connection; if the character is a lower-case letter, the response is interactive and is terminated by the LF character.

All transactions with the DAP-listener consist of a command followed by zero or more arguments separated by the space character, and double quotes may be used to prevent separation of tokens. The command set is taken from the DISH program and includes add, bind, compare, delete, fred, list, modify, modifyrdn, moveto, search, showentry, showname, squid and unbind. Commands and arguments are in lower case and may be abbreviated to any unique prefix.

There are two kinds of response. Numeric responses consist of arbitrary text. A response of 1 means the DAP transaction terminated normally; 2 means it failed; 3 means it was a search returning more than one result and one of the -hitone or -list option was selected; 4 means it terminated normally and the remainder of the line consists of the name of an entry; and 5 means all children of an entry were found. Once the response is completely sent, the DAP-listener closes the data connection. Although numeric responses use ASCII, they are not NVT-ASCII: the LF character is used to indicate end-of-line rather than the CR-LF line termination sequence.

Letter responses consist of brief text and expect further interaction from the client. The m response contains a one-line message to present to the user. The y response contains a yes or no question to present to the user, and the client answers with y or n followed by the LF character. The p response contains a password prompt, and the client answers with p followed by the password and the LF character. The e response asks the user to edit some text: it is followed by a decimal number of octets to be presented for editing, and the client answers with a single character, where e aborts the edit.

The l response contains an entry for a selection list, consisting of two strings separated by the dollar character, the first a user-friendly name and the second a fully-qualified Distinguished Name in textual format. The client acknowledges each one with l, and when it has collected them all it asks the user to select, then sends back L followed by one or more decimal numbers separated by spaces, the entry corresponding to the first response being numbered 1. The d response contains a name that the client may be interested in, in the same two-string form, and the client acknowledges it with d. The P response transmits a picture: it is followed by a decimal size, then three strings separated by the dollar character, naming the attribute, a user-friendly name and the Distinguished Name. The client answers with a single character, where P means the picture will not be sent, and otherwise the listener sends that number of octets, encoded using the PBM format from the PBMPLUS package.
sections.plainLanguage: The server answers with a single character that says what kind of answer it is: a number means it is finished, a letter means it needs something from the user first.

sections.title: An Example Interaction
sections.content:
The memo gives a worked example in which S refers to the DA-server, L to the DAP-listener, C to the client talking to the DA-server, and I to the client talking to the DAP-listener. The DA-server waits for a connection on TCP port 411, the client opens one, and the DAP-listener waits for connections of its own. The DA-server replies +OK 192.33.4.21 32867, giving the address and port of the data connection. The client opens that connection and sends bind -simple -user "@c=US@cn=Manager", and the DAP-listener replies with the name pc=US@cn=Manager, asking the client for a password. The client sends the password, and the DAP-listener closes the connection, signalling success but with no response. Since the response was null, the client verifies that the DAP-listener is still operating by sending STAT to the DA-server, which answers +OK.

The client then opens a new data connection and sends fred -expand "@" to list the top of the tree. The DAP-listener answers 5 and then a series of lines pairing a friendly name with a distinguished name, such as North America$l=North America and US$c=US, and closes the connection. A search for one person, fred -ufn rose,psi,us, returns 1 followed by much data. A search that matches several people, fred -ufn -list,rose,ps,us, produces a series of l responses, one for each match, each acknowledged with l. The client then sends L 2 to say that the second match was chosen, and the listener answers with a d response naming the entry followed by 4 and the data for that entry. Finally the client sends QUIT to the DA-server, the DAP-listener stops listening for connections, and the DA-server answers +OK.
sections.plainLanguage: The example walks through signing in, browsing the top of the tree, and picking one person out of a list of several.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says in one line that security considerations are not discussed in it. It is a description of an existing local mechanism, with no standard proposed and no analysis of the security of the arrangement.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss security at all.
